newsitem.title: DUBAI: UAE men sail to Iraq with food and medicine.
newsitem.headline: UAE men sail to Iraq with food and medicine.

text.p: A group of men from United Arab Emirates (UAE) sailed for Iraq on Wednesday with 32 tonnes of baby milk and medicine to help ease the suffering of Iraqi children under U.N. sanctions.

The white launch, bedecked with pictures of UAE President Sheikh Zaid bin Sultan al-Nahayan and the national white, red, green and black flag, left the port of Hamriyah in Dubai on the 38-hour trip to the southern Iraqi port of Khor al-Zubair.
It would be the first such visit since Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, organisers said. The UAE was a member of the U.S.-led coalition that drove Iraqi forces out of Kuwait in 1991.

What the organisers call the "first friendship trip" follows a November appeal by Sheikh Zaid to reconcile with Iraq and signs of growing Iraq-UAE trade after Iraq agreed to implement an oil-for-food deal with the United Nations last month.
But the organisers, a 10-man group of mostly bankers and businessmen, say it is a purely humanitarian mission with no political aims.
"We are only trying to help the Iraqi children who are suffering...we have no other considerations", Mohammad bin Abdullah bin Shabib, told Reuters.
UAE Defence Minister Sheikh Mohammad bin Rashid al-Maktoum, who is also crown prince of the emirate of Dubai, donated humanitarian supplies worth 1.5 million dirhams ($410,000).
"We told Sheikh Mohammad about our desire to help the Iraqi children and we won his support," bin Shabib added.

He said the group might embark on similar trips in the future. They are banking on pledges of support from local merchants before they sailed off and the start of the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan this week to raise future donations.

Another organiser said the group was armed with a letter from the Foreign Ministry approving their trip after clearing it with the United Nations and U.S.-led navy patrols in the Gulf enforcing the sanctions against Iraq.
The U.N. Children's Fund UNICEF said in November that 4,500 children were dying each month in Iraq from hunger and disease.
